newsitem.title: GERMANY: Eurocheques decline as German banks go electronic.
newsitem.headline: Eurocheques decline as German banks go electronic.

text.p: Eurocheques are facing a uncertain future as one of Germany's most popular means of paying for mid-sized transactions, as customers opt for cash or credit card, and banks seek lower processing costs.

A specially-commissioned study on German payments last week noted the steady decline in usage of eurocheques in favour of cash and credit cards and bankers said on Tuesday that the industry was debating how to respond.
But banks, especially those whose business is driven by traditionally plastic-averse retail customers, denied they had concerted plans to effectively scrap cheque-based transactions.

Banks decline to discuss the figures, but have been moving away from the expensive paper-based transaction processing needed for eurocheques towards the electronic systems on which credit cards and automated teller machines are based.

"We haven't actually reached a decision. Eurocheques are still an important payment method for many customers," Holger Berndt, board member at the German savings bank association, told a news conference in Bonn.

"We certainly are not at a point where we can say -- in half a year or a year there will be no eurocheques. But the past years have shown a decline in eurocheques, especially for people travelling abroad," a spokesman for the BVR co-operative banks association said separately.

Eurocheques, which each carry a guarantee for up to 400 marks, are widely used by Germans for small and medium-sized retail transactions and for foreign travel but credit cards and cash from automated teller machines are growing in popularity.

Processing firm GZS said Germans were involved in 15.5 million cross-border cheque transactions in 1996, down from 18.2 million the previous year, while the value of paper transactions dropped to 5.4 billion marks from 5.9 billion.
Credit card use, meanwhile, is booming, with market leader Eurocard posting a 16 percent rise in sales last year.
Bankers said it was too early to say what action they might take to curb eurocheque use.

The Handelsblatt daily newspaper reported on Tuesday that banks planned to stop guaranteeing eurocheques, stripping them of a large part of their attraction, but industry representatives dismissed this as premature and speculative.
"Whatever the decision is, it will not be binding," said a spokesman for the BdB group, which represents commercial banks.
Bankers are to meet over coming months to discuss the findings of the study as part of a working party on payments bringing in experts from all the main German banking groups.
